te: August twenty three, twenty twenty three. India lands a spacecraft near the south pole of the Moon.
No country had ever landed there before.
India builds its own nuclear submarines. It reached Mars on its very first try.
And yet... in hangars in Bengaluru and Nashik, brand new fighter jets are waiting.
Painted. Radars fitted. Almost ready.
But not one of these new jets has joined the Air Force yet.
The biggest reason? They are waiting for an engine. An engine made in Lynn, Massachusetts, about thirteen thousand kilometres away.
So here is the question. India landed on the Moon. Why can it not build its own fighter jet engine?

Welcome to Be Practical with Kishore. Today, the story of one of the hardest machines on Earth to build. Single crystal metal, broken promises, and a forty year fight to join one of the world's most closed clubs.
To understand why one engine matters so much, look at the Indian Air Force.
The Air Force is supposed to have forty two fighter squadrons. Today it has about twenty nine.
Old jets like the MiG twenty one have retired. New jets are needed, fast.
So in twenty twenty one, the government ordered eighty three Tejas Mark One A jets from Hindustan Aeronautics, HAL. In twenty twenty five, it ordered ninety seven more.
But HAL does not make the engine. Every one of these jets uses the F four zero four, made by GE Aerospace in America.
The engines were due from twenty twenty three. The first one came only in March twenty twenty five.
GE blamed problems in its supply chain. HAL put penalties on GE for the delay.
By October twenty twenty six, GE had sent only fourteen of the ninety nine engines. HAL says close to thirty jets are built and waiting.
Some testing work on radar and weapons is also still pending. But the engine has been the biggest hold up.
And a delay is only the small problem. The real danger is control.
India has been here before.
In May nineteen ninety eight, India tested nuclear weapons at Pokhran.
America answered with sanctions under a law called the Glenn Amendment.
Sales of the same GE F four zero four engines to India were stopped. American help on the Tejas flight controls also ended.
Indian engineers had to build the flight control system on their own. They did it.
The lesson was simple. If you do not own the engine, you do not fully own your fighter jet.
Nine countries have nuclear bombs. About ten have put a satellite in space with their own rocket.
But only a handful can design and build a modern fighter engine on their own. The main ones are America, Russia, Britain and France. And, after decades of struggle, China.
India tried to join this club. And that started one of the hardest engineering stories in its history.
In nineteen eighty six, Indian engineers began planning their own fighter engine.
The job went to the Gas Turbine Research Establishment, GTRE, a DRDO lab in Bengaluru. The engine was named Kaveri.
Full development was approved in March nineteen eighty nine, with a budget of about three hundred and eighty two crore rupees.
The plan was to finish by December nineteen ninety six.
The goal was huge. An engine that gives eighty one kilonewtons of push with the afterburner on.
And India was building a brand new jet, the Tejas, at the same time. Both almost from scratch. That doubled the risk.
When the Kaveri prototypes reached the test bench, the numbers did not add up.
It was meant to weigh eleven hundred kilos. It weighed twelve hundred and thirty five.
It was meant to push eighty one kilonewtons. As reported, it reached only about seventy.
And India had no facility to test a fighter engine in high altitude conditions.
So Indian engineers had to take the Kaveri to Russia for those tests.
The years went by. The Air Force could not wait for ever.
In September two thousand eight, the Kaveri was officially separated from the Tejas programme. The Tejas would fly with the American engine.
But GTRE did not stop. In twenty ten, a Kaveri flew for the first time, fitted to a Russian Ilyushin transport plane used as a flying test bed.
Twenty seven flights. Up to twelve kilometres high.
By twenty twelve, about two thousand crore rupees had been spent. The cost estimate had grown to over twenty eight hundred crore.
So why did it fail? To answer that, we need to go inside the engine.
